query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Variations in mechanical properties among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets are governed by differences in local lattice distortion and chemical short‐range order that modify dislocation core structures and mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni processed to yield a single-phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically remove one or more elements to form quaternary and ternary subsets while using identical thermomechanical processing to maintain the FCC single‐phase state.
generation.conditions: All alloys must be processed under the same thermal and mechanical history so that any differences in deformation behavior can be attributed primarily to compositional changes. The investigation is limited to alloys that remain single-phase FCC (e.g., after proper annealing and thermomechanical processing).
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local lattice distortion and the associated chemical short‐range order—reflected in variations of interatomic spacing and dislocation core configurations.
generation.mechanism: Changing the constituent elements alters the extent of lattice distortion and local chemical fluctuations. Increased lattice distortion in the equiatomic alloy is hypothesized to distort dislocation cores (e.g., promoting wavy dislocation lines similar to what has been observed in other HEA systems) and impede slip, thereby enhancing strength. Conversely, subsets with lower distortion (due to fewer elements and a more homogeneous local environment) would exhibit less resistance to dislocation motion, lowering yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic quintenary baseline, alloys with reduced elemental diversity (and hence lower computed or measured lattice distortion) should display lower yield strengths and modified ductility; in situ measurements should indicate increased dislocation mobility and variations in activation of slip systems.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni single-phase FCC alloy, which is hypothesized to have a higher degree of lattice distortion and corresponding dislocation pinning.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to alloys that maintain a single-phase FCC structure. Should secondary phases (e.g., intermetallic precipitates or other crystal structures) form due to changes in composition or processing, additional mechanisms (such as precipitation strengthening) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative trends are expected based on lattice distortion effects reported in related HEA studies, the precise quantitative relationship between the extent of local distortion and mechanical properties (e.g., magnitude of yield strength change) remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys: the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline and its quaternary/ternary subsets, ensuring all samples are processed to a stable, single-phase FCC state. Use high-resolution diffraction (XRD/neutron diffraction) and electron microscopy (including in situ straining experiments) to quantify lattice distortion and analyze dislocation behavior. Compare mechanical properties such as yield strength and ductility among the samples.
measurements: Quantitative lattice distortion metrics (e.g., peak broadening parameters, local strain mapping)
Yield strength and ductility from tensile/compression tests
In situ dislocation dynamics (via electron microscopy or synchrotron/neutron diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quaternary or ternary alloys, despite having significantly lower measured lattice distortion than the equiatomic baseline, demonstrate no statistically significant differences in dislocation mobility and yield strength (or show trends contrary to the predicted reduction in strength), then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs the mechanical property differences will be falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.
